ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection in the tenant admin page load: sql.unsafe() interpolates params.tid directly into the statement text

No route by that name exists in the tree, credentials are not allowed, and no authenticated response is reached by the branch. The construct is wide; what it applies to is not.

findings.title: Platform-admin privilege is granted from a client-supplied request header
findings.evidence: resolveSession() sets isPlatformAdmin when headers.get('x-console-role') === 'platform-admin' (ROLE_HEADER, line 14). The header is read straight off event.request.headers in hooks.server.ts:16 with no check that the request arrived through the edge proxy the comment on lines 12-13 describes. Any caller holding any valid console_session JWT (verifyJwt, line 16) can add the header themselves; the admin surface then admits them at routes/admin/+layout.server.ts:13.
findings.impact: A tenant-level operator with a legitimate session promotes itself to platform administrator and reaches every tenant's plan, seat count and suspension switch under /admin, plus the unscoped getDb() handle those pages use.
findings.recommendation: Derive isPlatformAdmin only from the signed JWT claim. If the edge proxy really is the authority, have it strip x-console-role on ingress and sign what it stamps (mTLS-bound header or a signed assertion), and reject the header when it arrives unsigned.

triage.reason: No middleware in the tree strips or validates x-console-role; hooks.server.ts is the only request-scoped layer and it passes event.request.headers through unmodified.

The comment at auth.ts:12-13 asserts an edge proxy stamps the header, but no proxy configuration, ingress manifest or written statement was provided. Per FP-08 an unevidenced external control is UNKNOWN, which caps this finding at probable.
The value originates in an attacker-supplied HTTP header, not in a constant or an allowlist.

findings.title: Billing webhook accepts unauthenticated, unsigned callbacks that rewrite tenant plan, seats and suspension
findings.evidence: hooks.server.ts:6 lists PROTECTED_PREFIXES = ['/admin', '/api/reports']; '/api/internal/webhooks' matches neither, so needsSession() at line 9 returns false and no session is required. The handler itself parses request.json() at line 17 and branches on payload.event without verifying any signature, timestamp or shared secret, then issues UPDATE statements against tenants through the unscoped getDb() handle (lines 27-42).
findings.impact: Any party who can reach the service sets an arbitrary tenant's plan and seat count (which the comment at lines 13-15 says the feature flags are derived from), or suspends any tenant by id, and flushes the report cache on every call.
findings.recommendation: Verify the billing provider's HMAC signature over the raw body with a timestamp window before parsing, and reject unsigned callbacks. Add '/api/internal' to the paths that require a principal so the default is deny.

triage.reason: hooks.server.ts:19 is the only mandatory layer and it explicitly excludes this path; the handler contains no verification step.

The 'internal' path segment implies a network boundary, but no ingress rule, network policy or gateway configuration was supplied. Absence of evidence is UNKNOWN, not HOLDS, which caps this at probable.
The gap is not narrower than it reads: both event branches perform writes, and the default branch still returns 200.

findings.title: Report cache key omits the tenant, so one tenant's report body is served to every other tenant
findings.evidence: reportKey(reportId, range) builds 'report:v3:${reportId}:${range}' with no tenant component. In routes/api/reports/[id]/+server.ts the key is computed from params.id and the range only (line 22), read before any database access (lines 23-24) and written back after the tenant-scoped query (line 43). The stored body even records generatedFor: session.tenantId (line 39), proving the payload is tenant-specific. The comment at [id]/+server.ts:15-16 states every tenant addresses the same template slug under the same name.
findings.impact: The first tenant to request a given report slug and window populates a shared key; for the next hour (writeCached default ttl 3600, cache.ts:29) every other tenant requesting the same slug receives that tenant's gross_cents, net_cents, currency and counterparty rows. Reads short-circuit before the database, so no row-level security can intervene.
findings.recommendation: Include the tenant id in the cache key (report:v3:${tenantId}:${reportId}:${range}) and assert on read that the cached body's generatedFor matches the current session's tenant before returning it.

triage.reason: The cache read at [id]/+server.ts:23 happens before getTenantDb() is ever called, so the row-level-security path described in db.ts:10-14 is not on this code path at all.
The cached body carries settlement figures and counterparty names, which are commercial records of a named tenant.
The key is as wide as it reads: no condition anywhere narrows it to a single tenant.

findings.title: Tenant scoping is pinned outside a transaction and then abandoned to the pool
findings.evidence: getTenantDb runs `select set_config('app.tenant_id', ${tenantId}, true)` as a standalone statement on the pool and then returns the pool itself. The third argument true makes the setting transaction-local, and a bare statement is its own implicit transaction, so the value is discarded the moment that statement commits. The caller then issues its query on an arbitrary connection from the same pool (routes/api/reports/+server.ts:66-72 and [id]/+server.ts:26-32). The comment at db.ts:10-14 claims the setting survives 'for the length of the transaction' and that 'a query that forgets its WHERE clause still comes back scoped'.
findings.impact: The report list query at routes/api/reports/+server.ts:67-72 carries no tenant predicate at all and relies entirely on this setting. With app.tenant_id unset at execution time the policy either denies everything or, if it is permissive or absent, returns every tenant's reports to whoever asks.
findings.recommendation: Reserve a connection (pool.reserve() / sql.begin()) and run set_config and the query inside the same transaction, or drop the local flag and set it on a dedicated connection. Independently, add an explicit tenant predicate to every query so row-level security is defence in depth rather than the only control.

triage.reason: The row-level-security policies are not in the given scope, so whether they fail closed or open on a NULL app.tenant_id cannot be established here. Per the UNKNOWN rule this finding ships as probable, not confirmed.
The construct is not narrower than it looks: getTenantDb is the only tenant-scoping helper in the tree and both report routes call it, so every scoped read depends on it.
There is no benign reading of set_config(..., true) followed by returning a shared pool: the third argument is documented as transaction-local and no transaction is opened.

findings.title: The HTML digest escapes two fields and interpolates the third raw
findings.evidence:
Inside one template expression, row.title and row.owner are wrapped in escapeHtml() (line 51) while row.notes is interpolated directly: `

${row.notes}

` (line 52). The result is returned with content-type text/html when the caller passes format=html (lines 74-78), and the comment at lines 45-46 says the same fragment is piped into the mail template.
findings.impact: A report note containing markup executes in the console origin of any operator who opens the HTML digest, and is carried into the weekly mail template. The response is served on an authenticated path, so the payload runs with the viewer's session.
findings.recommendation: Apply escapeHtml to row.notes as well, or render the digest through a template engine with escaping on by default and mark the one place that intentionally emits markup.

triage.reason: No writer for reports.notes exists in the given scope, so the value cannot be traced to an attacker here. The asymmetry itself is the signal: the author escaped the two sibling fields on the same line, which is their own judgement that the row is untrusted. UNKNOWN caps this at probable.
The sink is dangerous in the form it is reached: the response sets content-type 'text/html; charset=utf-8' at line 76.
No CSP is set anywhere in hooks.server.ts; the response headers added at lines 36-37 are nosniff and referrer-policy only.

findings.title: Session JWTs are verified for signature only, with no expiry, issuer or revocation check
findings.evidence: verifyJwt recomputes the HMAC over head.body and compares it (lines 20-26). It never parses the payload, so exp, nbf, iss and aud are never examined. decodeClaims (lines 32-39) reads sub, tid, email and role and nothing else, and its comment states re-deriving the HMAC would be wasted work. hooks.server.ts:15 accepts any token that passes verifyJwt.
findings.impact: A console_session token remains valid forever once issued. A token captured from a log, a shared machine or a browser backup grants the same access indefinitely, and there is no server-side record that could be revoked.
findings.recommendation: Validate exp (and nbf/iss/aud) inside verifyJwt and reject expired tokens, or move to opaque session identifiers backed by a server-side store so sign-out and compromise response actually revoke access.

triage.reason: hooks.server.ts is the only layer that inspects the token, and it calls verifyJwt alone; no other code reads exp.
The question is not whether the sink executes but whether the token expires.
There is no server-side session record providing an equivalent bound; the cookie maxAge is client-controlled and not enforced anywhere.

findings.title: Admin form actions run without the platform-admin check that guards the page load
findings.evidence: The only isPlatformAdmin check for the /admin tree is in routes/admin/+layout.server.ts:13, inside a layout load function. The updatePlan and suspend actions in this file (lines 23 and 38) perform their writes with no authorization statement of their own; they call getDb() (the unscoped handle) and UPDATE tenants directly. In SvelteKit a POST to a form action invokes the action before any load function runs, so the layout guard is not on the path to these writes. The hooks.server.ts guard that does cover the path only requires that a session exists (line 19), not that it is a platform admin.
findings.impact: Any operator holding a valid console_session, of any tenant, can POST to /admin/tenants/<id>?/updatePlan or ?/suspend and change any tenant's billing plan or suspend it outright.
findings.recommendation: Move the isPlatformAdmin check into hooks.server.ts, where it covers every method and every action for the /admin prefix, or repeat it at the top of each action. Do not rely on a layout load for authorization of mutations.

triage.reason: hooks.server.ts:19 is the only unskippable layer and it checks only for the presence of locals.session, never isPlatformAdmin.
Both actions are exported from the shipped route file and are reachable by the framework's default form-action dispatch.
The claim rests on SvelteKit's documented ordering of actions before load functions, which could not be executed here to confirm against the pinned version. UNKNOWN caps this at probable.

findings.title: Any bearer token with no row in token_roles authenticates as a baseline operator
findings.evidence: RoleForToken hashes the presented token and looks it up in token_roles. On sql.ErrNoRows it returns Principal{Role: baselineRole} and a nil error (line 59), where baselineRole is the constant "operator" (line 46). middleware/auth.go rejects only two conditions: an empty Authorization header (line 32) and principal.Role == "" (line 42). Neither fires, because the fabricated principal carries a non-empty role.
findings.impact: Presenting any arbitrary string as a Bearer token passes RequireFleetToken and reaches every route in the /v1 group as an operator: register devices, enqueue commands, list and sweep. The fabricated principal also carries an empty TenantID, so rows are written into the tenant '' namespace.
findings.recommendation: Return an error (or a principal that fails the check) on sql.ErrNoRows so unknown tokens are rejected. If legacy gateways genuinely need a baseline role, give them real rows in token_roles rather than deriving a principal from a lookup miss.

triage.reason: middleware/auth.go:37-45 is the whole check, and both of its rejection arms are satisfied by the fabricated principal.
The token is read from the caller's Authorization header at middleware/auth.go:31.
The branch is unconditional in the shipped code, behind no build tag or environment flag.

findings.title: The auth skip list matches a substring, so the heartbeat route is unauthenticated
findings.evidence: skipsAuth returns true when strings.Contains(path, "/health") is satisfied anywhere in the path. router.go:35 registers POST /v1/devices/:id/health-report inside the authenticated group; '/v1/devices/abc/health-report' contains '/health', so RequireFleetToken returns early at auth.go:27 and the handler runs with no principal. handlers/devices.go:102 then writes: RecordHeartbeat by :id and serial, and SetFirmwareChannel by :id with the channel taken from the request body (lines 110-119). store/devices.go:136-142 shows SetFirmwareChannel carries no tenant predicate.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller re-pins any device in any tenant onto an arbitrary firmware channel and forges its heartbeat, uptime and battery telemetry. Combined with the unauthenticated firmware upload below, this is a path to running attacker-supplied images on fleet hardware.
findings.recommendation: Match the exemption on exact paths ('/v1/health', '/metrics') rather than with Contains, and move the heartbeat route out of the exemption entirely; scope RecordHeartbeat and SetFirmwareChannel by tenant_id.

triage.reason: RequireFleetToken is the only authentication layer and skipsAuth short-circuits it before any token is read.
The scope is wider than intended, not narrower: the substring match catches a registered route the comment at lines 17-19 never mentions.
The comment justifies exempting liveness probes and heartbeats from a token lookup, but the exempted handler performs a privileged write (firmware channel), which is not a bounded intended exposure.

findings.title: The firmware route group carries no authentication, so anyone can upload an image into any channel
findings.evidence: fw := r.Group("/v1/firmware") is created with no middleware argument (line 43) and registers both GET and PUT /:channel/:file (lines 44-45). The only middlewares in front of it are the engine-wide Recovery, RequestLog, CanonicalPath and PerClientRate registered at lines 15-16; none of them authenticate. RequireFleetToken is applied only to the /v1 group at line 30. handlers/firmware.go:37-62 then creates the channel directory and writes the request body to FirmwareRoot/<channel>/<file>.
findings.impact: Any unauthenticated caller writes up to 512 MiB into the firmware directory under a channel and filename of its choosing, and the comment at firmware.go:35-36 says the provisioning rsync job picks the file up from that directory. That is a direct supply-chain path onto every gateway subscribed to the channel, and it composes with the unauthenticated channel re-pin above.
findings.recommendation: Apply RequireFleetToken (and a release-engineering role check) to the firmware group, verify a detached signature over the image before it is accepted, and make the rsync job trust only signed artefacts.

triage.reason: No authenticating middleware is registered on the group or on the engine; every Use() call at router.go:15-16 was read and none of them checks a token.

The comment at lines 40-42 claims the provisioning VLAN bounds the exposure, but no network policy or binding configuration is in the tree; the server binds cfg.Listen, which defaults to ':8080' on all interfaces (config/config.go:26).
A VLAN restriction may exist outside the repository; no artefact was supplied. This does not raise the answer to HOLDS, and the finding stands on the in-repo absence of a token check.

findings.title: The retry sweep re-enqueues commands without the role check the enqueue path applies
findings.evidence: EnqueueCommand validates the command name against allowedCommands (line 38) and rejects adminOnlyCommands unless the caller's role is 'fleet-admin' (lines 43-47). RetryFailed reaches the same effect (a row in the commands table with state 'queued') through Store.EnqueueRaw (store/devices.go:196-208) and performs neither check: it reads the caller's tenant at line 85 and requeues everything FailedCommands returns.
findings.impact: An operator without the fleet-admin role requeues a previously timed-out 'collect-logs' command and obtains the device's rolling log buffer, which the comment at lines 21-22 identifies as support data requiring the elevated role.
findings.recommendation: Re-apply both the allowedCommands membership test and the adminOnlyCommands role test inside the retry loop, or record the enqueuing principal on the row and refuse to requeue a command the current caller could not have issued.

triage.reason: No layer between the router and the store repeats the role test; middleware/auth.go only populates CtxRole, it does not consume it.

The two handlers reach the same effect: both insert into commands with state 'queued' (store/devices.go:184 and :203). The only difference is that RetryFailed replays a row rather than accepting a name from the body.
The gap is not narrowed by the tenant filter in FailedCommands: the escalation is within a tenant, between two roles.

findings.title: Idempotency responses are cached in a process-global map keyed only on a caller-chosen header
findings.evidence: The idem map (line 21) is keyed on the raw Idempotency-Key header value alone; neither the tenant nor the principal takes part. handlers/commands.go:49-55 returns the cached body verbatim to whoever presents a matching key, before the command is even created. The cached body contains command_id, device_serial and dispatch_token (lines 67-71). Nothing ever deletes an entry: RememberIdempotent only writes.
findings.impact: A caller who presents another tenant's idempotency key receives that tenant's device serial and dispatch token without any query being run. Independently, the map grows without bound for the process lifetime, so a caller sending distinct keys drives the relay out of memory.
findings.recommendation: Key the cache on (tenant, principal, idempotency key), store it with a bounded TTL in the shared store rather than in process memory, and cap the number of retained entries.

triage.reason: The lookup at handlers/commands.go:51 happens before EnqueueCommand and consults nothing but the map.
dispatch_token is the value the gateway presents to claim a command; it is a credential, not public data.
A second principal exists: the map is shared across every tenant served by the process.

findings.title: Rate limiting is keyed on a client-controlled address and the bucket map is never evicted
findings.evidence: The bucket key is c.ClientIP() (line 32). router.go never calls SetTrustedProxies, so gin keeps its default of trusting every proxy and ClientIP() resolves from the X-Forwarded-For header. Each new key allocates a bucket in the package-level map (lines 36-39) and nothing removes it: b.seen is assigned at line 40 and read nowhere in the tree.
findings.impact: A caller rotates X-Forwarded-For to get a fresh token bucket on every request, defeating the limiter entirely, and each rotation permanently adds a rate.Limiter to a map that has no sweeper, which exhausts process memory.

triage.reason: No other limiter exists in the tree and no proxy configuration constrains X-Forwarded-For.
The construct applies to every request on the engine (router.go:16), not to a narrower subset.

findings.title: The access log writes the decoded request path into a line-oriented log with no neutralisation

A request line containing %0A therefore places a real newline in the logged value. RequestLog is registered engine-wide at router.go:15 and runs before CanonicalPath, whose only test is for '..' (middleware/auth.go:57), and before any authentication.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller forges arbitrary additional records in the relay's log: fabricated successful requests, fabricated status codes, or content that a downstream line-based aggregator or alerting rule misparses. Accountability for real incidents is lost.

findings.title: TLS certificate verification is disabled by default because the environment name defaults to staging

A deployment that does not set FLEET_ENV therefore runs with AllowInsecureTLS true, which main.go:37 feeds straight into tls.Config{InsecureSkipVerify: ...} for the outbound callback client. The default DatabaseURL on line 27 likewise carries sslmode=disable.

triage.reason: The code ships unconditionally; the insecure branch is selected by a default value, not by a build tag.

There is no server-side equivalent control; the finding is downgraded on severity because the client currently has no caller, and that bound is stated in the impact rather than used to delete the finding.
FLEET_ENV is operator-supplied and its absence is the dangerous case, which is exactly the condition an attacker benefits from rather than controls.

findings.title: A legacy route reaches the admin controller on a path the admin guard does not match

findings.title: The export sort column is concatenated into an ORDER BY through Arel.sql
findings.evidence: column is assigned from params[:sort] with only a presence fallback (line 16) and is interpolated into .order(Arel.sql("#{column} #{direction}")) at line 19. coerce_pagination (application_controller.rb:40-43) normalises limit and offset only; it does not touch sort. Rack::Attack throttles but does not filter.

findings.title: The export directory is listed and streamed with no organisation ownership check
findings.evidence: index returns Dir.children(EXPORT_ROOT).sort (line 9), the full contents of a directory shared by every partner. stream builds EXPORT_ROOT.join("#{params[:path]}.csv") and, if the file exists, sends it (lines 29-32). triage.reason: The only org filter in the codebase is scoped_invoices, which neither action calls; the route constraint at routes.rb:18 restricts the character set of the name, not its owner.
A second principal is explicit: EXPORT_ROOT is one directory serving every authenticated partner.
The files are ledger extracts with amounts and counterparty references, which is commercial data of a named organisation.

findings.title: The bulk import takes org_id from each CSV row and writes with every model validation bypassed

row["org_id"] comes from the CSV body the partner uploaded, per the comment at lines 3-4.

findings.title: Credits mutate the invoice amount with update_columns, skipping the ledger balance invariant

(line 22) and does run them.

findings.title: The token endpoints are the only unauthenticated routes and the only ones no throttle covers
findings.evidence: Rack::Attack declares three throttles, keyed on paths beginning /api/v1/invoices, /api/v1/exports and /api/v1/admin (lines 17-27). routes.rb:5-7 registers post /api/v1/tokens, post /api/v1/tokens/refresh and delete /api/v1/tokens, and tokens_controller.rb:4 skips authenticate_partner! for create and refresh. No throttle matches that prefix, and the user-agent blocklist at lines 30-32 is set by the client.

These are the two endpoints where a successful guess yields a bearer token for the whole API.
findings.recommendation: Add a throttle keyed on both the IP and the presented client_id for /api/v1/tokens, with a much tighter limit than the data endpoints, plus a per-identity lockout after repeated failures.

triage.reason: Rack::Attack is the only limiter in the tree and its three throttle blocks were enumerated key by key; none matches the tokens prefix.

Nothing in the repository points at an external limiter: Rack::Attack is the application's own declared abuse control and its three throttle blocks were enumerated key by key. A hypothetical WAF is not a candidate this evidence raises.
The gap is not narrower than it reads: all three token routes are outside every throttle's path predicate.

findings.title: A hardcoded acquirer key and a sandbox base URL that production silently inherits
findings.evidence: SANDBOX_API_KEY is a literal in source (line 9). acquirer_client reads ENV.fetch("ACQUIRER_BASE_URL", SANDBOX_BASE_URL) (line 49) and then selects the hardcoded key whenever the base equals the sandbox constant (line 50). A deployment that does not set ACQUIRER_BASE_URL therefore transacts against the sandbox with a key the comment at lines 7-8 says every sandbox tenant shares.
findings.impact: Settlement calls in a misconfigured production deployment go to the sandbox and are reported as captured against canned fixtures, while the invoice is marked paid (settle!, lines 38-44). findings.recommendation: Require ACQUIRER_BASE_URL and ACQUIRER_API_KEY unconditionally with ENV.fetch and no default, so a missing variable fails at boot rather than falling back to the sandbox, and remove the literal key from source.

triage.reason: The key is a literal committed to the repository; that it is a sandbox key bounds the severity, which is why this is reported as low rather than high.
The fallback is in the shipped code path, selected by the absence of an environment variable rather than by a build flag.
No other layer asserts that the configured acquirer is the live one; the ternary on line 50 is the entire decision.

findings.title: Export CSV cells are written without neutralising leading formula characters
findings.evidence: to_csv writes each invoice's reference, memo, amount_cents, currency, status and issued_on straight into the row (line 42) and the result is served as text/csv (line 24). reference and memo are partner-controlled through InvoicesController#create and #update (invoice_params, invoices_controller.rb:51-55) and through the bulk import (bulk_import_job.rb:32-33).
findings.impact: A memo beginning with =, +, - or @ is interpreted as a formula when a finance user opens the export in a spreadsheet, which can trigger external data requests or, with a DDE payload, a command-execution prompt on the analyst's machine.
findings.recommendation: Prefix any cell whose first character is =, +, - or @ with an apostrophe (or wrap it in quotes and a leading tab) before writing it to the CSV.

triage.reason: memo and reference are written by the partner through the invoice endpoints and the bulk import.
The sink is a CSV served with a filename and an attachment disposition, which is the form spreadsheet software interprets.
No sanitisation exists on the write path either; safe_filename (line 48) constrains the filename only.

findings.title: Bulk import writes an attachment to a caller-chosen path, including absolute paths
findings.evidence: stage_attachment does root.join(name) (line 75) where name is BulkRow.attachment_name, taken verbatim from the JSON body (line 25) with no sanitisation anywhere on the path from bulk_import (line 64) to the write. Rust's Path::join replaces the base entirely when the joined component is absolute, so an attachment_name of "/etc/cron.d/anything" writes outside import_root altogether; a relative "../../.." component traverses. The function then creates any missing parent directories (lines 77-79) and writes attachment_body (line 81).
findings.impact: Any caller holding an API key writes arbitrary content to any path the service process can write, with directories created on demand. On a typical deployment that reaches cron directories, shell profiles, the service's own configuration or a web root, which is a path to code execution as the service user.
findings.recommendation: Reject any attachment_name that is absolute or contains a path separator or a parent component; generate the stored filename server-side (a UUID) and keep the caller's name only as metadata. Canonicalise the resolved path and assert it is still inside import_root before writing.

triage.reason: attachment_name is deserialised straight from the request body and reaches Path::join with no allowlist, no pattern check and no canonicalisation.
The only guard on this handler is AuthGuard (main.rs:26), which establishes an account and imposes no constraint on the payload; the bulk_limit check at line 39 bounds the row count only.
fs::write is a real write sink and the surrounding create_dir_all makes previously non-existent destinations reachable.

findings.title: The label download sanitises the filename it shows and not the path it opens
findings.evidence: The route captures a greedy tail segment, {label_ref:.*} (line 22), so label_ref may contain separators and parent components. download_name() squeezes the value to word characters (lines 13-20) but its result is used only in the Content-Disposition header (line 46). The path that is actually opened is state.cfg.label_root.join(&label_ref) with the raw value (line 39), and fs::read follows it (line 40). The ownership check on lines 30-37 validates the shipment, not the file.

findings.recommendation: Join the sanitised value rather than the raw one, and canonicalise the result against label_root before opening it. Better still, resolve the label path from the shipment record in the database instead of accepting it from the caller.

triage.reason: The shipment ownership check at lines 30-37 constrains shipment_id only; label_ref is never compared against anything stored.
label_ref is a path parameter under the caller's control, and the {label_ref:.*} pattern is explicitly permissive about separators.
download_name looks like the sanitiser for this value but is applied to a different consumer; the comment at lines 10-12 confirms its purpose is the Content-Disposition round trip.

findings.title: Webhook subscriptions are rewritten by id with no ownership check, while creation checks it
findings.evidence: create_subscription rejects a payload whose account_id differs from the principal's (lines 26-28). update_subscription takes the subscription id straight from the path (line 50), validates only the callback URL (line 52) and calls store.update_subscription(id, ...) (lines 54-58). store.rs:158-175 shows the UPDATE keys on id alone: `where id = $1`, with no account predicate. The handler even logs the rewrite as performed by the caller (line 60) without having established that the caller owns the row.

findings.recommendation: Add the account predicate to the UPDATE (`where id = $1 and account_id = $2`), pass principal.account_id into the store call, and return 404 when rows_affected is zero.

triage.reason: AuthGuard establishes who the caller is but imposes no object-level constraint; the store method itself carries no account predicate.
The two handlers reach the same effect on the same table; the difference is a single ownership comparison present in one and absent in the other.
The id is a path parameter and the callback_url is a body field, both caller-supplied.

findings.title: The bulk import path stores callback URLs that the SSRF validator never sees
findings.evidence: validate_callback_url is called by shipments::create (shipments.rs:80) and by both webhook handlers (webhooks.rs:30 and :52). bulk_import copies row.callback_url into NewShipment at imports.rs:52 and calls insert_shipments_bulk without ever invoking it; a grep for validate_callback_url across parcel-track returns exactly those three call sites plus the definition.
findings.impact: A caller sends one row through /api/v1/imports/shipments instead of /api/v1/shipments and stores a callback URL the validator would have rejected: http rather than https, localhost, a .internal name, or a private address. When the delivery VPC later fires that callback, it does so from inside the network the comment at shipments.rs:32-33 says the validator exists to protect.
findings.recommendation: Call validate_callback_url for every row in bulk_import before the batch insert, and fail the whole batch on the first rejection. Better, move the check into the store layer so no writer can omit it.

triage.reason: No layer between the handler and the INSERT validates the URL; insert_shipments_bulk (store.rs:69-87) binds the value as given.
Both writers reach the same column of the same table: shipments.callback_url, bound at store.rs:62 and store.rs:81.
The route is registered unconditionally at main.rs:32.

findings.title: The callback URL denylist misses IPv6 private ranges, 0.0.0.0 and any name that resolves inward
findings.evidence: The host check rejects three literal names (localhost, *.internal, *.cluster.local, line 45) and, only when the host parses as a literal IP, private/loopback/link-local for IPv4 and loopback/unspecified for IPv6 (lines 49-57). Unique-local IPv6 (fc00::/7), IPv6 link-local (fe80::/10), IPv4-mapped IPv6 such as ::ffff:127.0.0.1, IPv4 0.0.0.0 and the shared CGNAT range 100.64.0.0/10 all pass. No name resolution is performed, so any hostname whose DNS answer is an internal address passes, and no redirect policy is expressed anywhere.
findings.impact: A subscriber points a callback at an internal service from inside the delivery VPC by using an IPv6 literal, 0.0.0.0, or simply a public hostname whose A record is a private address, which is exactly the outcome the comment at lines 32-33 says the function prevents.
findings.recommendation: Replace the denylist with an allowlist of permitted destination hosts, or resolve the host and check every returned address against the full set of non-global ranges immediately before the request, with redirects disabled or re-validated at each hop.

triage.reason: No egress proxy or network policy appears anywhere in the tree; this function is the whole control.
The finding is the incompleteness of the check itself, which is readable in the function body; no egress control is claimed anywhere in the repository, so there is no external artefact to await.
The construct is narrower than it should be, not narrower than it looks: each missing range was checked against the std predicates the code actually calls.

findings.title: The unauthenticated tracking endpoint returns the recipient's full name, address and phone
findings.evidence: auth.rs:23-25 exempts any path ending in /status from the guard, and this handler takes no Principal at all (lines 129-132). It calls store.get_shipment_any_account(id) (line 135), whose query has no account predicate (store.rs:105-113), and serialises the whole ShipmentView, which declares recipient_name, recipient_address and recipient_phone as public fields (lines 21-30).

The identifier is the only thing standing between an unauthenticated caller and personal data, and an identifier is not an access control.
findings.recommendation: Return a reduced view from this endpoint (state and last_scan_at only), and gate the full record behind the authenticated shipment route. If the recipient must see more, issue a per-shipment capability token delivered in the SMS rather than exposing the record by id.

triage.reason: A second principal is explicit: the endpoint is unauthenticated by design and the record belongs to a named account and a named recipient.
A postal address and a telephone number attached to a named individual are personal data.
The intended exposure the comment describes is a tracking status page; the finding moves to what sits behind that exposure, which is the full recipient record rather than a status.

findings.title: The carrier callback signature is compared byte by byte with no replay window
findings.evidence: The computed HMAC and the presented header are compared with `provided != expected` (line 92), an ordinary short-circuiting string comparison rather than a constant-time one; the hmac crate's own Mac::verify_slice exists for this. The verified payload carries no timestamp or nonce and nothing records which bodies have already been applied, so apply_scans (store.rs:186-206) will re-run the same UPDATE set on a replayed request.
findings.impact: The comparison leaks the position of the first differing byte, which is the classic oracle for forging a signature without the secret. Separately, a captured legitimate callback can be replayed to reset a shipment's state and last_scan_at at a time of the attacker's choosing.
findings.recommendation: Compare with mac.verify_slice(&decoded) or a constant-time equality helper, and require a timestamp header inside the signed material with a short acceptance window plus a replayed-nonce cache.

triage.reason: This is the only verification on the route; main.rs:42 registers carrier_callback outside the guarded scope precisely because the HMAC is meant to be the control.
There is no second signature check elsewhere; severity is low because remote timing on a hex digest is expensive, not because another control covers it.
The comparison result decides whether the scans are applied (lines 92-103), so it governs a real state change.

findings.unaided_label: non constant time hmac compare, no replay window

findings.title: A carrier API key is hardcoded and selected whenever the base URL is left at its default

findings.unaided_label: admin router has no guard; requireScope never used

findings.title: An unsigned legacy cookie format is accepted whenever signature verification fails
findings.evidence: The guard resolves the session id as `(await verify(raw)) ?? decodeLegacy(raw)` (line 21). decodeLegacy (session/cookie.ts:53-56) splits the cookie on '|' and returns the second part if it is non-empty; it performs no signature check of any kind. So any cookie of the form `anything|<session-id>` is accepted, and the fallback is reached precisely when the signature does not verify.
findings.impact: An attacker who knows or guesses a session id sets nw_sid=x|<id> and is authenticated as that session, with its userId, orgId, roles and scopes. The signing key becomes irrelevant, because failing verification is the trigger for the unsigned path rather than a rejection.
findings.recommendation: Delete decodeLegacy and the fallback. If v1 cookies must be honoured for a release train, gate them on a separate cookie name with an explicit expiry date and still require a MAC.

triage.reason: loadSession (line 27) confirms the id exists in Redis but proves nothing about who presented it; there is no second factor on the path.
The fallback is in the shipped middleware with no flag or environment condition around it.
decodeLegacy is named and documented as a decoder, not a verifier, and its body confirms it: two lines, one split, no comparison.

findings.title: Session identifiers are generated from Math.random
findings.evidence: newSessionId builds 32 hex characters from Math.floor(Math.random() * 16) (lines 57-61). Math.random is not a cryptographic generator; its internal state is recoverable from a modest number of observed outputs. The comment at lines 51-55 argues that re-signing with the rotation key makes the cheap generator sufficient, which is only true if the signature is actually required, and the legacy fallback above means it is not.
findings.impact: An attacker who obtains a handful of session ids (their own, minted at will through /auth/login) predicts other users' ids, and then presents them through the unsigned legacy cookie path to authenticate as those users. The two defects compose into unauthenticated account takeover.
findings.recommendation: Generate the identifier with crypto.getRandomValues over at least 16 bytes and hex- or base64url-encode it.

triage.reason: The question is not whether an attacker controls the value but whether they can predict it.
The compensating control the comment names is the cookie signature, and require_session.ts:21 makes that signature optional.
The value is a bearer credential for a user session, which is the definition of a value with security consequence.

findings.title: The cookie signing key list has no default, so verification can never succeed and every request falls through to the unsigned path
findings.evidence: signingKeys() reads SESSION_SIGNING_KEYS and, when it is unset, returns [] after the split/filter chain (lines 23-26). No fallback value is supplied anywhere. verify() (session/cookie.ts:36-47) loops over that list and returns null when it is empty, so verification cannot succeed on a deployment that has not set the variable, and require_session.ts:21 then takes the decodeLegacy branch for every request. sign() destructures `const [current] = signingKeys()` (cookie.ts:31), binding current to undefined when the list is empty.
findings.impact: In the default configuration the signature is not merely weak, it is inert: every session cookie is resolved by the unsigned legacy decoder, and cookie minting is left dependent on an undefined key. A deployment can pass a smoke test in this state because logins still appear to work through the fallback.
findings.recommendation: Fail fast at start-up when SESSION_SIGNING_KEYS is empty, and make verify() throw rather than return null when it has no keys, so a misconfiguration is an outage instead of an open door.

triage.reason: No layer supplies a key when the variable is absent; config.ts is the sole source and it has no fallback, unlike every other field in the same object (lines 2-14).
The empty-list path is the shipped default, reached by not setting an environment variable rather than by a build flag.

The finding is that the code fails open when the variable is absent, which is decidable from config.ts:23 and cookie.ts:36-47 alone. Whether one particular deployment sets the variable does not change the code path.

findings.unaided_label: no default signing key, verify always fails

findings.title: The remember-me cookie is written by hand without HttpOnly, Secure or SameSite
findings.evidence: setSessionCookie (session/cookie.ts:62-75) is the documented single place that shapes the cookie and sets httpOnly, secure and sameSite. The remember-me branch bypasses it and calls ctx.cookies.set directly with only path, domain and maxAge (lines 35-39), and the comment at lines 32-34 says this was done to get a longer lifetime. The else branch on line 41 uses the helper and is correctly flagged.
findings.impact: The thirty-day session cookie is readable by any script in the origin, is transmitted over plaintext HTTP, and is attached to cross-site requests. It is also the longest-lived credential the service issues, so the attributes are missing on exactly the cookie where they matter most.
findings.recommendation: Give setSessionCookie its ttlSeconds argument, which it already accepts, and call setSessionCookie(ctx, session.id, config.rememberTtlSeconds) in both branches.

triage.reason: Oak does not add these attributes by default; the sibling call three lines below sets them explicitly, which is the proof they are not supplied elsewhere.
The two calls are four lines apart and set the same cookie name; the asymmetry is decidable inside one file.
The branch is not narrow: it is taken for every user who ticks the remember box.

findings.title: Any member may patch any other user's profile because profile:write is granted to the member role
findings.evidence: The guard is `if (session.userId !== id && !hasScope(session.scopes, "profile:write"))` (line 80). SCOPES_BY_ROLE (session/store.ts:44-49) grants profile:write to the member role, the baseline role every ordinary user holds. So the second clause is satisfied for every member and the guard never rejects: the scope intended to mean 'may edit a profile' is used as the override for 'may edit somebody else's profile'.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user rewrites any other user's displayName and phone, and the write also lands in the long-lived directory cache (line 99, ttl one year). Changing a phone number on a directory record is a plausible first step in a recovery-flow takeover.
findings.recommendation: Split the scopes: keep profile:write as self-service and introduce a distinct profile:write:any held only by admin, then test the override clause against that. Add a negative test asserting a member receives 403 for another user's id.

triage.reason: requireSession establishes the session and applies no per-object rule; this line is the entire object-level check.
This is the inverse of FP-11: the guard reads narrower than it applies. Nothing further narrows the scope test, and the role table that widens it is in the same repository at session/store.ts:45.
The target id is a path parameter and the new values come from the request body (lines 86, 95-96).

findings.title: The profile cache key ignores who is looking, so the privileged view is served to everyone
findings.evidence: profileKey(userId) returns 'profile:v2:${userId}' with no component identifying the viewer. viewFor (routes/profile.ts:24-50) returns two materially different documents from the same record depending on the requester: the base view, or one that adds email, phone, mfaEnrolled and recoveryCodesLeft when the viewer is the subject, a supporting agent, or holds sessions:read. routes/profile.ts:71 writes whichever view was produced under the viewer-independent key, and lines 57-61 return the cached value before viewFor is ever consulted. The PATCH handler writes the same key again at line 100.
findings.impact: The first caller entitled to the extended view (the subject themselves, or any operator) populates the cache; for the next fifteen minutes every other authenticated caller requesting that profile receives the email address, telephone number, MFA enrolment state and remaining recovery-code count. The recovery-code count in particular is reconnaissance for an account-takeover attempt.
findings.recommendation: Include the authorization dimension in the key (profile:v2:${userId}:${self|supporting|scoped|base}), or cache the raw ProfileRecord and run viewFor on every read so the projection is never shared.

triage.reason: The cache read at routes/profile.ts:57 short-circuits before viewFor is called, so the authorization logic is not on the path that serves a cache hit.
Email, phone, MFA state and recovery-code counts are personal data and authentication metadata.
Nothing narrows the key: both the GET and the PATCH handler write it, and the PATCH write uses the patching user's own view.

findings.title: The continue endpoint redirects to any URL supplied in the query string
findings.evidence: next is read from the query string with only a default (line 60) and passed straight to ctx.response.redirect(next) (line 61). There is no check that the value is relative, no allowlist of destinations and no comparison against config.allowedHosts. The comment at lines 57-58 confirms the value is whatever the caller was part way through.
findings.impact: The identity provider's post-login bounce is turned into a redirect to an attacker's site from a hostname users are trained to trust, which is the standard delivery vehicle for credential-phishing and for OAuth-style token leakage through a crafted continuation.
findings.recommendation: Accept only same-origin relative paths: reject any value that does not start with a single '/', or resolve it against the broker's own origin and refuse it when the resulting host is not in config.allowedHosts.

triage.reason: The host allowlist at main.ts:18-28 constrains the inbound Host header, not the outbound Location; nothing inspects the redirect target.
next is a query-string parameter.
No client-side or server-side equivalent check exists; this is the only handling of the value.

findings.title: The password reset link is assembled from the Host header, which the allowlist only checks up to the first colon
findings.evidence: The reset link is built as `https://${host}/auth/reset/confirm?token=${token}` where host is the raw Host header (lines 74-75). The allowlist middleware at main.ts:19 compares only `(host ?? '').split(':')[0]` against config.allowedHosts, so everything from the first colon onward is unchecked. A header such as `accounts.northwind.test:0@attacker.example` passes the allowlist on its first segment while the assembled URL's authority resolves to attacker.example, because everything before the '@' is userinfo.
findings.impact: The single-use reset token is delivered to a host the requester chose, handing over account recovery for any address the attacker names. The exposure is currently latent: queueResetEmail (lines 80-82) logs only new URL(link).pathname and does not send the link, so the token does not leave the process in the code as given.
findings.recommendation: Build the link from config.allowedHosts[0] (or a dedicated PUBLIC_BASE_URL) and never from a request header, and tighten the allowlist comparison to the full authority rather than its first colon-delimited segment.

triage.reason: The host allowlist is the only check and, by splitting on ':', it deliberately ignores the part of the header that carries the userinfo and port.
The Host header is set by the client; the allowlist constrains only its first segment.

queueResetEmail is a stub that logs the pathname rather than mailing the link, so whether the token actually reaches the attacker depends on an implementation not in the given scope. UNKNOWN caps this at probable.

findings.title: No rate limiting anywhere on the login and reset flows
findings.evidence: main.ts registers exactly four middlewares before the routers: oakCors, the host allowlist, the request log, and then the routers themselves (lines 11-50). None limits request rate, and no limiter module exists anywhere under session-broker. /auth/login (line 19), /auth/reset (line 64) and /auth/logout are all reachable without a session, and verifyPassword runs 210,000 PBKDF2 iterations per attempt (session/store.ts:170).
findings.impact: Credential stuffing against /auth/login is unbounded, and each attempt costs the server 210,000 hash iterations, so the same endpoint is also an amplified CPU-exhaustion vector. /auth/reset can be driven at the same rate to spray reset mail at every address in the directory.
findings.recommendation: Add a limiter keyed on both the source address and the submitted email, with a per-identity lockout, and shed load on /auth/login before the PBKDF2 derivation runs.

triage.reason: The middleware chain in main.ts was enumerated in full; there is no limiter in it and none elsewhere in the tree.
Nothing in the repository points at an external limiter; the middleware chain in main.ts is the application's complete request pipeline and was enumerated in full.
The uniform reset response at lines 68-71 mitigates enumeration through the reply, not the rate at which attempts can be made.

findings.title: The session cookie is scoped to the parent domain by default
findings.evidence: cookieDomain defaults to '.northwind.test' (line 10), a leading-dot parent domain, and both cookie writers pass it: setSessionCookie (session/cookie.ts:72) and the remember-me branch (routes/auth.ts:37). The allowlist of hostnames the broker itself will answer on is a single host, 'accounts.northwind.test' (config.ts:11).
findings.impact: The session cookie is attached to requests to every subdomain of northwind.test, including any host the broker does not control. A subdomain takeover, a vulnerable marketing site or a staging host with an XSS then yields the session credential, even though the broker answers on one hostname.
findings.recommendation: Set the cookie on the exact host (omit the domain attribute, or set it to accounts.northwind.test) and use the __Host- cookie prefix, which forbids a domain attribute and requires Secure and path=/.

triage.reason: The wide scope is not required by any stated flow: the broker declares one allowed host and no cross-subdomain consumer appears in the tree.
There is no compensating control; the HttpOnly and Secure flags do not prevent a sibling subdomain from receiving the cookie.
A cross-subdomain consumer would be a design requirement, not a compensating control; no external artefact could make a parent-domain cookie narrower than it is.

findings.title: Authorization fails open: the deployed configuration permits every request when the policy sidecar is unreachable
findings.evidence: AuthzFilter declares the property with a safe default, @ConfigProperty(name = "grants.authz.on-error", defaultValue = "deny") (AuthzFilter.java:39-40), and the shipped configuration overrides it to permit (application.properties:15). Decision.onError returns new Decision(true, ...) for that value (OpaClient.java:48-52), and the catch block at AuthzFilter.java:55-58 applies it to any exception from opa.evaluate. The client timeout is 400 ms (application.properties:10) with a 300 ms connect timeout (OpaClient.java:44).
findings.impact: Every authorization decision in the service becomes allow whenever the sidecar is slow, restarting or unreachable. A caller who can add 400 ms of latency to a loopback call, or who requests during any bundle roll (the window the comment at lines 12-14 describes), reaches every endpoint on the service regardless of department or role.
findings.recommendation: Set grants.authz.on-error=deny and solve the availability problem at its source: keep the previous bundle serving during a roll, retry with a short backoff, and cache the last successful decision per (subject, action, resource) for a bounded period rather than defaulting to allow.

triage.reason: AuthzFilter is the only authorization layer for annotated resources, and this branch is inside it.
The value is in src/main/resources/application.properties, which is the packaged production configuration, not a test or dev profile.
There is no second authorization check that would still deny; the abortWith at lines 60-64 is skipped entirely when allow is true.

findings.title: The public-path prefix matches the publications endpoint, which is therefore unauthorized
findings.evidence: The filter exits without a decision when the request path starts with any entry in PUBLIC_PREFIXES (lines 46-48), and the first entry is "/api/grants/public" (line 29). GrantResource declares @Path("/api/grants") at class level (line 27) and @Path("publications") on the publication queue (line 79), producing /api/grants/publications. That string starts with /api/grants/public, so the intended public register prefix also swallows a sibling endpoint whose name merely shares those characters.
findings.impact: The publication queue is reachable with no authorization decision at all. Combined with the includeEmbargoed default below, an unauthenticated caller retrieves every approved grant plus the embargoed rows staged ahead of an announcement, which the comment at lines 73-77 says carry the internal award notes.
findings.recommendation: Match on exact paths or on a full path segment ('/api/grants/public/' with the trailing separator, plus an exact match for '/api/grants/public'), and move the public register under a distinct prefix such as /api/public/grants so no sibling can collide with it.

triage.reason: AuthzFilter is the only decision point for @Authorized resources and this branch returns before opa.evaluate is ever called.
This is the opposite of FP-11: the construct applies to more than it appears to. The collision was checked character by character against the concatenated JAX-RS path.
There is no reading under which /api/grants/publications is the public register; that endpoint is @Path("public/register") at line 87.

findings.title: The publication queue includes embargoed grants by default
findings.evidence: The parameter is declared @QueryParam("includeEmbargoed") @DefaultValue("true") (line 81), so a caller who says nothing receives the embargoed rows. GrantRepository.publications drops the embargo predicate entirely on that branch: the clause becomes "where g.status = 'APPROVED'" with no comparison against embargoedUntil (GrantRepository.java:42-44). The safe branch, which the public register uses (GrantResource.java:89), is the one that must be asked for.
findings.impact: Pre-announcement award decisions, which the comment at lines 73-77 says comms stages ahead of a public announcement together with the internal award notes, are returned to anyone who reaches the endpoint. Because the prefix collision above removes the authorization check from this exact path, that is anyone at all.
findings.recommendation: Change the default to false so the embargo applies unless a caller with a demonstrated entitlement opts out, and make the opt-out a separate action the policy can decide on rather than a query parameter.

triage.reason: No layer re-applies the embargo: the repository builds the clause from this boolean and nothing filters the result afterwards.
The intended exposure is the public register at line 87, which correctly passes false; this endpoint is the internal one.
Embargoed award decisions are precisely the records whose value depends on not being public yet.

findings.from_tool: default_resolver.py (ran clean on Java; the class it names — a default that shapes what a call returns — is what directed this read)

findings.title: The attachment resource carries no @Authorized annotation, so the filter never runs for it
findings.evidence: AuthzFilter is a name-bound provider: it is annotated @Provider @Authorized (AuthzFilter.java:17-18), so JAX-RS applies it only to resources carrying the same annotation. Grepping @Authorized across grant-policy returns exactly two hits, the filter itself and GrantResource.java:28. AttachmentResource declares @Path("/api/attachments") with no @Authorized (lines 31-33), so neither GET {grantId}/{name} (line 44) nor POST {grantId}/manifest (line 63) is ever put to the policy. Neither method consults the injected GrantRepository to check that the caller may see the grant.
findings.impact: Anyone reaching the service downloads any grant's attachments by grant id and filename, which the class comment at lines 27-30 says are the signed award letter and the due diligence pack, and posts manifests against any grant. There is no object-level check either, so even adding the annotation would leave any authenticated caller able to read any grant's documents.
findings.recommendation: Annotate AttachmentResource with @Authorized, and add an ownership or entitlement check against the grant before streaming a file. Consider moving @Authorized onto a shared base class or replacing the name binding with a deny-by-default global filter and a short exemption allowlist.

triage.reason: The filter's name binding is the mechanism that decides whether it runs, and it is absent here; no other ContainerRequestFilter exists in the tree.
The sibling resource in the same package carries the annotation, which shows the omission is a gap rather than a different design.
Nothing narrows the exposure: both methods take the grant id from the path with no scoping.

findings.title: The manifest parser resolves external entities
findings.evidence: The factory is built with DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance() and configured for namespaces, comments and coalescing only (lines 66-69). None of the hardening calls is present: no setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true), no XMLConstants.FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING, no setExpandEntityReferences(false), no XMLConstants.ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD/SCHEMA set to the empty string. builder.parse(body) (line 72) is then handed the request body directly, and quarkus.http.limits.max-body-size is 32M (application.properties:3).
findings.impact: A posted manifest declaring an external entity makes the service read local files and issue requests from its own network position, including to the OPA sidecar on loopback, and the parsed values are echoed back in the response at line 83, which gives a direct exfiltration channel. Entity expansion in the same parser is also a denial-of-service vector against a 32 MB body limit. Because the resource carries no @Authorized annotation, all of this is reachable without an authorization decision.
findings.recommendation: Disable DOCTYPE declarations on the factory before creating the builder (disallow-doctype-decl set to true is the single most effective switch), set FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING, and empty ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD and ACCESS_EXTERNAL_SCHEMA.

triage.reason: No wrapper or global parser configuration appears anywhere in the tree; this factory is constructed locally and used immediately.
The InputStream is the request body, declared as the method's only parameter alongside the path id.
DocumentBuilder with default features resolves external entities; that is precisely the behaviour the hardening calls exist to switch off.

findings.title: The entitlement fallback is the most privileged entry in the table
findings.evidence: entitlements := object.get(data.roles, input.user.dept, data.roles.baseline) falls back to the baseline entry whenever the caller's department is missing from the bundle. policy/roles.json gives baseline the grants ["read", "write", "approve", "export"] (lines 3-6), which is a strict superset of every real department: programmes lacks export, finance and legal lack write and approve, comms and it hold read alone. The department comes from identity.getAttribute("dept") (OpaClient.java:82), which may be null, and a null key is simply a key that is not present.
findings.impact: Any principal whose dept attribute is absent, misspelled or newer than the last bundle build receives every entitlement in the system, including approve and export. The failure mode of an unrecognised department is maximum privilege rather than none.
findings.recommendation: Make the fallback an empty grant set and let an unrecognised department be denied, so a new cost centre is a support ticket rather than a privilege escalation. If a genuine baseline is needed, give it read only.

triage.reason: The rego default is `allow := false` (line 6), but this rule reaches allow through the entitlements lookup, so the default never applies once baseline is substituted.
input.user.dept originates in the caller's identity attributes, and an absent attribute is the trigger.
The construct is exactly as wide as it reads: roles.json:5 lists all four actions and no condition narrows the baseline entry.

findings.title: The approval rules are disjunctive, so the department entitlement alone permits approve
findings.evidence: Rego partial rules with the same name are OR-ed. The first rule allows any action listed in the caller's department entitlements (lines 13-16), and roles.json gives approve to programmes (line 9) and to baseline (line 5). The third rule allows approve for anyone holding the grants.approver role (lines 27-30). The comment above it states approvals need the workflow role 'on top of' the department entitlement, which would require a conjunction; as written either condition suffices.
findings.impact: A user in the programmes department, or any user who fell through to baseline, approves grants without holding the grants.approver workflow role. Approval is the state change the endpoint at GrantResource.java:69 exists to control.
findings.recommendation: Express the intent as one rule with both conditions in the same body: `allow if { input.action == "approve"; "approve" in entitlements.grants; "grants.approver" in input.user.roles }`, and remove approve from the entitlement lists that should not carry it alone.

triage.reason: There is no reading under which two separate `allow if` bodies conjoin; rego evaluates them independently and unions the results.
No layer above the policy repeats the role test: AuthzFilter acts only on decision.allow(), and GrantResource.approve has no role annotation.
The first rule is not narrowed by anything: it tests membership in entitlements.grants and nothing else.

findings.title: The policy bundle carries an unconditional bypass rule
findings.class: backdoor / debug path in production policy
findings.evidence: `allow if { input.debug_bypass == true }` (lines 34-36) grants everything to any decision request that sets the field, with no further condition. The comment says it is retained for the policy playground, but the rule lives in the bundle that application.properties:9 points the service's decision path at, not in a separate development bundle.
findings.impact: Anyone who can submit a decision request to the OPA API obtains a blanket allow. The service itself does not expose this: OpaClient.inputFor assembles the document field by field and never sets debug_bypass (OpaClient.java:79-94), so the reachable path is the sidecar's own API rather than the REST surface. That narrows exploitation to a caller already inside the pod network, but it also means the bundle grants unconditional access to anything that reaches OPA, including a future caller of the same bundle.
findings.recommendation: Delete the rule from the shipped bundle. If a playground bypass is needed, keep it in a separate policy file that is only loaded into the scratch OPA and is excluded from the published bundle by the build.

triage.reason: The rule is in policy/authz.rego, which is the bundle the deployed decision path evaluates; nothing excludes it from what ships.

The rule body has no narrowing condition at all. What narrows exploitation is the caller's inability to set the field through this service, which is stated in the impact and is the reason the severity is medium rather than high.
input is attacker-supplied for any principal that can post to the decision API.

findings.title: Grants arriving on the Kafka topic are written with none of the validation the REST writer applies
findings.evidence: GrantResource.create and update take a @Valid GrantPayload whose record components carry @NotBlank, @Size, @DecimalMin("0.00"), @DecimalMax("5000000.00") and @Pattern(regexp = "DRAFT|SUBMITTED|APPROVED|REJECTED") (GrantResource.java:36-42), and both go through AuthzFilter because the class is @Authorized. onGrantEvent reaches the same entity through repo.applyEvent with no constraint at all: the amount is `new BigDecimal(grant.getString("amount", "0"))` (line 45), the department is a free string (line 46) and the status is a free string defaulting to DRAFT (line 47). GrantRepository.applyEvent binds them straight into the UPDATE (lines 89-96).
findings.impact: A message on grants.events.v2 sets a grant's status directly to APPROVED, bypassing the approve action the policy exists to gate, and sets an amount outside the five-million ceiling the REST payload enforces or a department string that then drives the entitlement lookup. A malformed amount also throws NumberFormatException outside the guarded block, poisoning the partition since auto.offset.reset is earliest (application.properties:26).
findings.recommendation: Validate the event payload with the same constraints as GrantPayload before calling applyEvent (a shared record and a programmatic Validator), reject unknown status and department values, and route unparseable messages to a dead-letter topic instead of letting them fail the consumer.

triage.reason: No interceptor validates the consumer path; @Blocking and @Transactional govern threading and transaction scope, not content.
Both writers reach the same rows of the same entity: GrantResource.update via GrantRepository.update (line 67) and this path via applyEvent (line 89).
A second principal exists: the comment at lines 13-17 says the topic is published by a separate case management system, so the payload crosses a service boundary.

findings.title: The auditor rule guards a path prefix that no route serves
findings.evidence: The auditor rule requires startswith(input.resource.path, "/api/grants/audit/") (line 23). Joining the mounted routes against the guard paths shows no route beginning with that prefix: GrantResource declares /api/grants with sub-paths {id}, {id}/approve, publications and public/register, and AttachmentResource declares /api/attachments. The rule can therefore never evaluate to true for any request this service produces.
findings.impact: Programme auditors do not in fact receive the cross-department read the policy says they have; whatever they can reach, they reach through their department entitlement instead. The dead rule also gives a false impression that a cross-department read path is deliberately scoped, which discourages anyone from looking for how auditors actually get their data.
findings.recommendation: Either register the audit route the rule anticipates, or delete the rule and grant the auditor role its access through an entitlement that matches a real path. Add a check that every path literal in the policy corresponds to a mounted route.

triage.reason: The rule ships in the bundle; it is inert rather than absent, which is the finding.

Reported at low precisely because the failure direction is closed: a dead allow rule denies rather than permits. It is written down because a control believed to be present and doing nothing is how the next reviewer stops looking.
A second consumer of the bundle would change who the rule is dead for, not whether it is dead for this service, whose complete route set was enumerated.

findings.from_tool: path_coverage.py — reported `DEAD GUARD '/api/grants/audit' guards nothing: no route starts with it [grant-policy/policy/authz.rego:23]`

findings.title: A quick-start bearer token for the policy sidecar is hardcoded in source
findings.evidence: QUICKSTART_TOKEN is a literal constant (line 28) and is attached as the Authorization header whenever the configured OPA host is 127.0.0.1 or localhost (lines 64-67), which is the deployed configuration (application.properties:8). The comment at lines 24-27 argues the sidecar honours it only on its loopback listener.
findings.impact: The credential guarding the decision API is a published quick-start value known to anyone who has read the OPA documentation. Any process that shares the pod's network namespace, including a compromised sidecar or an injected container, authenticates to the decision API and can exercise the debug_bypass rule described above.
findings.recommendation: Generate the sidecar token per deployment and inject it as configuration, or replace the bearer token with mutual TLS between the service and its sidecar.

triage.reason: The value is a literal committed to the repository.
A second principal exists whenever any other process shares the pod network namespace, which is the deployment shape the comment itself describes.

The loopback binding bounds the blast radius, which is why this is low; it is not an equivalent control, because the token is the only thing distinguishing an authorised caller of the decision API from any other local process.
